The big ‘real’ issue is that Skynet learns and gains power absurdly fast at first, and then stalls out at exactly the level where it can somehow be defeated by a John Connor and a ragtag group of survivors, because otherwise the time loop would not close and also we do not have a movie or franchise. This is the typical Hollywood ‘intelligence stops doing anything, and also the AI’s efforts stop scaling, at exactly the point where the humans can still barely win’ which exists for reasons that should be obvious, both in Hollywood and also in the real debates over AI. People like humans winning, and people like telling human stories. Please Review This Podcast Many solid choices by Dean Ball. For me this splits into ‘things that I can confirm are very good’ and ‘things I have not listened to and thus it is hard to say but they have good company.’ I am especially a fan, from this list, of Cognitive Revolution, Conversations with Tyler, Odd Lots, Dwarkesh Podcast, Money Stuff and Complex Systems. Dwarkesh suffers from being ‘too good’ so I end up often reading transcripts instead. I sometimes listen to Lex Fridman and 80,000 Hours, as well as AXRP, but long pod is long and I choose topics. Dean W. Ball: i doubt anyone cares but here are my most listened to podcasts so far this year. many of the hosts of these shows follow me and you should know I think you’re awesome, even if we have never met or spoken. Anastasia Gamick: Dean, where does this free time come from?? Dean W. Ball: I don’t sleep very much At some point I will write about at least some of my favorite podcasts. Two not here that I very much enjoy are Wait Wait, Don’t Tell Me and Serious Trouble, and I at least sometimes listen to EconTalk, Clearer Thinking, Win-Win and Plain English. There are also some that fall into a different category of gaming and entertainment. It can’t all be work stuff. My favorite Magic podcast is All Tings Considered, but that is constrained by my ‘I do not know what the new cards do’ problem. Gamers Gonna Game Game Game Game Game You can now report players on Magic the Gathering: Arena. There are five complaints: Inactivity, Hate Speech, Inappropriate Username, Verbal Abuse and Spamming. Three of these seem silly given the lack of communication channels. But it is very good to be able to report players for Inactivity, also known as stalling, which players do either because they are mad at you, because they can or in the hopes that you will give up or accidentally time out. Andrea Mengucci proposes ways to help bring back competitive Magic, including more focus on Pauper as a cheap format. I’m ‘out of the game’ in all senses, so it’s hard for me to evaluate the current situation, but the obvious thing is that Magic is huge yet they give you very little to strive for. Every reasonable solution starts with running real tournaments, with strong prizes, and ways to accumulate points, qualify for things and earn money, pride and titles, including room for some people to be Pros off of results rather than streaming. Wizards is not doing this because they don’t care, not because they do not know how. I guess they do not like money. I Was Promised Flying Self-Driving Cars Human Progress: Swiss Re, one of the world’s leading reinsurers, found that Waymo’s autonomous vehicles generated 88% fewer property damage claims and 92% fewer bodily injury claims than human-driven vehicles. On September 1, Waymo opened service in Denver, San Diego and Tampa. Waymo once again expands its approved service area in Greater San Francisco as well as Los Angeles. Most of this region will be waiting for a while, but this means Waymo will have no trouble finding good uses its cars for a while no matter what happens elsewhere. I continue to eagerly await Waymo coming to East Bay, given that is where I usually visit. Alas, the odds look bad, and say a majority of the time this won’t happen even in 2027. Complaints are the prices remain too high, which is another way of saying demand exceeds supply. Tesla asks for permits for 5,000 robotaxis in Las Vegas, was initially given 10 but has now been approved for the full 5,000. Waymo and Uber each got 1,000. There are some things self-driving cars probably won’t ever do for you. Nate Silver: Robotaxis are very cool but there’s probably going to be a weird equilibrium where human drivers have some competitive advantage because they’re less strict about following speed limits and traffic laws. Mike Solana: waymo already increased aggression. down in LA, especially, drivers wouldn’t let them out of four-way stops. you can feel the difference on the roads, now, even as a pedestrian. they’re not the docile creatures they were last year. Misha: Waymo will never truly replace human cab drivers until I can flag one down, jump in and shout “Follow that car! Step on it!” Waymo gets into an accident that makes the news. As one would expect, it is minor contact and entirely not the Waymo’s fault. Not to be outdone, Waymo ‘nearly ran over’ a two-year old, said many. This is the framing people go with for ‘actual nothing happened and it was not close.’ SFist: A father in Noe Valley says a Waymo robotaxi stopped within 13 feet of his two-year-old daughter when she fell in the crosswalk, nearly running her over, but Waymo claims the car wouldn’t have hit her. Alex Immerman: “Waymo nearly ran over a 2-year-old” is an irresponsible framing. The Waymo stopped 13 feet away. Two king size mattresses placed end-to-end fit between. If my kid fell in a crosswalk, I’d be terrified. I’d also be grateful the approaching car was a Waymo. Divia Eden : I think cars with superhuman breaking are part of what might make the world way safer for kids to roam, and they can’t arrive soon enough IMO! ‘I literally don’t know what you want from me’ very much applies here. The Waymo did exactly what you would want it to do, complete with displaying ‘pedestrian yield,’ and the complaint seems to be that the father was worried that it might not do that? Yes, I very much worry that one accident will ruin everything. Eventually there will be one accident. Government Working I will never understand the idea that it is good and right to arrest people for making edgy jokes in a private WhatsApp group, without anyone in the group even minding, as happens in the UK. How does anyone describe this as anything but utter insanity? Flock cameras plus AI is coming, while Flock demos things like ‘how to monitor a protest in real time.’ Have we considered not allowing the creation of a dystopian surveillance network for the government or others to hook up to their AIs? Mamdani (Again) Fails Economics Forever I will keep harping on the Mamdani NYC city-run grocery store fiasco, mainly because it is funny. Dan Rivoli: Lead official for Mayor Mamdani’s NYC Groceries tells me city may give grants to local grocers fearing competition from city-run stores “policies and programs, grants, incentives that can come alongside these grocery stores to support other local independent businesses” Dan Rivoli: Clean up, aisle 5. Spokesman for @NYCEDC , which oversees NYC Groceries for Mayor Mamdani, sent me a statement today saying: “We are not currently considering any grant programs” for grocers competing with city stores, but rather tax abatements and zoning benefits Catherine Rampell: Hear me out. What if instead of selling food below cost to all comers at taxpayer expense, and then using more taxpayer dollars to subsidize private companies that can’t compete with those prices, we had a program that targeted nutritional assistance just to the people who needed it, as a supplement? We could call it, I don’t know, supplemental nutritional assistance To those who think 115th & Park is a “food desert”: I have an Aldi, Costco, Shop Fair, Whole Foods, Foodtown, CTown, Food Bazaar, and Target to sell you Here is 115th & Park, where the new store presumably will go: Dan Rivoli: This is the second time a key part of NYC Groceries had to be walked back. First was when an official said there would be a “library card-esque” system to prevent resale. After reasonable inference that ID would be required, mayor himself had to say no ID would be required They keep changing their story because there are zero ways to implement the thing they want that do not end in disaster. Variously Effective Altruism Remember what the benchmark is, in two parts. Part 1: The super rich do things like pay a specialty agency $100,000 per year with a $1 million spending minimum above that, and then spend absurd amounts of money on whims and momentary thrills, and most of all on getting exactly the things they want whenever they want them, and yes they are often jaded. Olivia Ferney, a travel specialist they hire, confirms, as we learn in How To Make A Killing, that you might want to think this means they are miserable, but actually the super rich are happy with the results, thank you very much. I totally get it, especially the part where you have a person you can call that makes happen whatever you want to happen. Must be nice. But I’d feel sick about it, and not only because I could have given the money away. I sometimes wonder how many extra zeroes I’d need on my net worth before I’d feel entitled to start acting like this. At least two, but less than five. Part 2: Yonan: Seth Rogen says his financial fear is dying with $10 million in the bank that he could have spent while he was alive. “I’m afraid I’m going to die with too much money. I don’t have children, and I’m afraid I’m going to die and be like, I could have had a place at the beach” “I don’t want to die with like $10,000,000 in the bank that I could have spent doing fun, alive things” “A jet to Paris on a whim? Yeah, exactly. I could have been jetting. I could have been jetting this whole time” This, on the other hand, feels completely insane, even if you have Too Much Money. Which Seth Rogen clearly does. Costs are not benefits, and the point of having money is partly to spend it but also to have the peace of mind that it is there when you need it. The value of that extra $10 million spent while rich is a tiny fraction of how much you would miss it if you lived longer than you expect while in any danger of being poor. Dying with nothing in the bank, or close to nothing, is a huge disaster, far worse for Seth Rogan than dying with $10 million. That’s even if you discount that you could use the money to actually help people. So, yeah, I criticize it a lot, but maybe this whole ‘effective altruism’ thing is actually pretty good. How Sarah Constantin thinks about evaluating grant applications, here condensed with a slight Zvi slant to the explanations, as we think highly similarly here. I endorse basically all of this. It’s the donor’s money, spend it on what the donor cares about. Importance, neglectedness, tractability. Yay community infrastructure, especially for the donor’s community. Yay niche topics, that matter to the donor. Yay ‘technical’ work, involving rare unfakeable skill, like making a thing. Yay straightforward public information resources. Yay ‘cool shit’ even if there isn’t an obvious payoff beyond being cool. Two cheers for meta. Keep a mix of meta and object level. Gumption counts. If the person wants to do it, there is a reason. Yay personal relationships. Use your local knowledge, including of people. Check ideological orientation, in case it interacts with the project. Filter slop aggressively. Do not waste our time. Yay outcomes that are concrete and legible, not always but it helps. Invest rather than donate where that would make sense. If Hell does not exist, then we do not need to create it. We already have New Jersey. A highly underrated charity strategy is Give Effective People Money, especially retroactive funding for things you loved, with no strings attached. Also speed kills. Chris Lakin: if you’re capital looking for philanthropic stuff to fund… consider retroactively funding work that already happened that you loved. give those people no-strings funds to do more whimsical stuff (or do whatever they want) without requiring them to waste time on applications AND you build reputation for yourself as the serious funder to be connected to. (there are too many funders who say they’re “interested” in funding xyz, but never actually do anything, so you could build a great reputation really quick) Charles: I did this once (gave somebody with a good track record ~£30k to buy out their time so they could focus on whatever they thought most valuable vs whatever paid at the time) but Jan Tallinn then gave them like 10x that a few months later (not due to anything that happened in between I think) so the counterfactual impact was pretty low. Chris Lakin: Wdym seems like you got them started multiple months earlier? That’s huge Charles: Nah the lag on the money arriving due to EA regrantor lag meant I don’t think they actually had the money yet Moral intuitions very different from my own, remember that this was asking ‘what do others do’ not ‘what should people do’: Robin Hanson: According to poll, relative strength of moral guides others use: Robin was as usual Robin Hansoning, as he described reason as ‘argued for by our impressive thinkers’ rather than ‘what the person thinks is right, based on their own reason.’ As you would expect, Robin then argues hard against using your conscience. A very clear case for Effective Altruism, especially from Patrick McKenzie: Kelsey Piper: I’m an effective altruist because 1) I care a lot about how I can best use my money and time to achieve my goals in the world, and EAs wrote a lot of the stuff I found useful on that topic and 2) EA told me in the 2010s to worry about AI and pandemics, and they were right. Patrick McKenzie: I wouldn’t self-identify as an EA, and if one hypothetically read the Day 6 Vaccinate CA memo, one would find language in it which resonated with EAs and one would find language in it which resonated with Tolkien. If I can be permitted to make personal empirical observations: 100% of funders who have expressed regret they did not fund VaccinateCA themselves self-identify as EA. 100% of funders who have contacted me post VaccinateCA offering to backfill money I personally donated the organization self-identify as EA. Given base rates among college-educated Americans, EAs were _wildly_ overrepresented among early volunteers and coordinators. Even adjusting for the tech industry lineage/seed set/theory of change I think this remains true. People who are reasonably read as barometers of community opinion tell me that VaccinateCA is wildly impressive evidence of efficacy in their community, with respect to EAs. No person in the California government or public health field has ever said this to me directly. (I will report, for completeness’ sake, that I have been told through an intermediary that the _writeup_ of VaccinateCA was considered above-replacement-rate for a postmortem by a senior official in public health. I offered a meeting. EAs have taken meetings w/ me.) The Lighter Side Sometimes I have sympathy for people who lose money but if you bought Hunter Biden’s $LAPTOP right before it crashed 98% within an hour of its launch then I do not really know what you were expecting. Spotted on Letterboxd about La La Land, some people are a tough crowd: Clayton Petty: Louvre. Immediately. In case anyone was wondering, yes, I will also always think like this. Proof by counterexample: Cheat, cheat, cheat, cheat, cheat. IYKYK, if not see here. Roger Blumenthal: Trending on social media Fable argued hard that no, Michigan did not actually lose to The Bye (aka Western Michigan) and that there really was a mysterious extra second on the True Stadium Clock that allowed Michigan to have one more play. Uh huh.

If you live in the US and purchased an iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model between June 10th, 2024, and March 29th, 2025, you can file a claim on the settlement's website, as reported earlier by MacRumors. You can receive an estimated $25 per eligible device, but the settlement's website notes that this can increase to $95 depending on how many people file claims. items.title: Review: Neagley is a worthy spinoff to megahit Reacher
items.author: Jennifer Ouellette
items.content: Prime Video looks to have another hit on its hands with Neagley, a new spinoff series set in the same universe as the streaming platform’s critically acclaimed Reacher, now in its fourth season. Both shows are solidly addictive escapist fare, and while Neagley has some uneven elements, it mostly sticks to the successful formula while exploring new ground to give a very different main character her due. (Some spoilers below, but no major reveals.) Reacher fans will already be familiar with Frances Neagley, played to perfection by Maria Sten (Swamp Thing). She’s arguably the most diehard friend of former US Army military police officer turned drifter Jack Reacher (Alan Ritchson), coming to his aid again and again as he confronts a bevy of dangerous criminals over four hugely entertaining seasons. (Of course Ritchson’s Reacher makes an appearance in an opening scene, lending his muscle to rescue a kidnapped child.)Read full article Comments

items.title: Can John Ternus find Apple’s next big thing?
items.author: Nilay Patel
items.content: Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On. Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. But this event was special, for a number of reasons. It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. The timing of those two things was not at all coincidental, as you’ll hear Mark explain. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously. This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era. Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. Welcome to Decoder. Good to be here finally. Thanks for having me. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple. Yeah, I’m really excited to talk to you. Obviously, Apple just had its big event. They announced the iPhone Duo. It was John Ternus’s first event as CEO. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple. There’s been a lot of shuffling. You’ve been chronicling them very, very deeply over the past few years. Let’s just start with the event. I have a very basic question for you. Sure. Do you ever get nostalgic for a time when you didn’t know what was going to happen at the iPhone event? Do I ever get nostalgic? Do you ever wish that you, Mark Gurman, were about to be surprised? Honestly, I never think about it that way. I’m just fixated on delivering the goods and delivering the news. And people love their Apple. People want to know everything that’s coming down to the last minute, so I’m here to provide it for them. The thing with me, and I don’t know if most people know this about me, but I hope people know this about me, is that I’m a huge Apple fan through and through, and I’ve always been. And I’m so lucky to be able to cover a company that I love, a company that I am obsessed with, and a company whose products I use. There are so many people who cover companies that they couldn’t care less about. That’s not me. So I do what I do because I love Apple and I love covering Apple. I love the community around it, and I love talking about it. And it’s always fun to get a peek at the future and help keep not only myself informed, but people informed around me. That actually leads me to a lot of things because I’ve known you forever. We’ve been working in and around the same spaces forever. You got your start as an Apple blogger at the Apple rumor sites. There’s a whole culture around Apple that has grown up and changed over the years, and you can trace it to different eras of hardware, to different CEOs, to different sizes of the company. This was the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Apple announced a big new product in the iPhone Duo. Do you sense that the community is changing? How do you think that community has changed over the years? And do you think Ternus is going to lead to a difference in what that community feels like? I have to say, this event really didn’t feel much different than a Tim Cook event. They felt pretty interchangeable. It could have been Tim up there introducing it. It could have been Ternus up there introducing it. The one thing I will say that did feel slightly different is that Ternus came out swinging with a point of view on AI. The first thing he came out with was about the intelligent personal hub. Now, here’s the big difference between Tim Cook and John Ternus in terms of their management style. You’re inside Apple, you’re an executive, you’ll come to him with an idea, you’ll come to him with a viewpoint, a decision, an opinion, and he’ll just pepper you with more questions. He won’t make a singular decision in many cases. It’s very much communal decision-making, collaborative decision-making. John Ternus, if you come to him and you want him to make a decision, he’ll make a decision. He’ll have an opinion. Now, you may hate his opinion; you may completely disagree with him, but he has a viewpoint. But that’s the big difference between talking to people about Ternus and Tim. Ternus comes out talking about his view on AI. I may disagree with it. A lot of people may disagree with it. They may think the OpenAI or Anthropic approach is superior, but at least he came out and had a viewpoint. Apple’s been at this AI game now for two years since they launched Apple Intelligence at WWDC in 2024, and it’s been a mishmash of things. They haven’t really come out with a very strong narrative and viewpoint, and they finally did. So, as I said, whether you agree with it or not, they did do that. And I thought that was a really interesting way to kick off the keynote. All right, we’re just going to get into the weeds of Apple nerds disagreeing about things. Okay, let’s do it. I sat through that event, and I appreciated the same thing that you saw, which is, “Oh, we’re telling a story.” John Ternus is on the stage, and the first thing he’s doing is telling a story about this product and how it fits into the universe of technology. And then I took a beat, and I was like, oh, but they’re also just making sure that he’s successful at his first event by playing Apple’s greatest hits. Because an “intelligent personal hub” is just a replay of Steve Jobs saying the iMac was the digital hub. At the very end of the event, Ternus said, “There’s one more thing, and it’s the iPhone Duo.” There was just a part of all of that that, to me, felt like Apple saying, “Look, our new CEO can put on the clothes of the old CEO. He can do this same dance that you’re expecting.” Underneath it, what I felt was, to your point, that I don’t buy the story about the intelligent hub. No, I don’t buy it either. Because any of the things we’re seeing AI do are happening in cloud services. It’s the same week that Meta launched Muse, right? Right. You can feel what you want about Meta launching Muse, but Mark Zuckerberg is giving everybody 8GB of storage and 8GB of RAM in the cloud, and Muse can go do a lot of things that AI on the iPhone absolutely cannot do at this point in time. I just felt like there was a part where they were playing it really safe with John by having him basically show up and be the new lead singer of Journey. You can’t get it wrong if you’re going to do “Lights.” If you’re going to show up on stage and do “Don’t Stop Believin’,” you’re going to be fine for a minute. And it’s all the stuff that comes after that’s going to really show his real personality. But it sounds like you thought that that’s his point of view. Well, it’s a couple of things. At a very high level, Apple’s going to tell a story around what they have. If Apple invented ChatGPT, they would’ve invented ChatGPT, and they would’ve told a good story around that. Apple has gone as far as it’s able to, at least for now, on AI. So it’s telling the story, the best version of that story that they can with what they have to work with, with the bird they have in hand. So that’s the one thing. I agree with you on the intelligent personal hub, and how that compares to the iMac back in ’98. And it feels like they’re trying to sell this pivot from the Mac as the center of everything with the peripherals around it; then you got to iCloud in 2011, the center of everything with the peripherals around it. Now, it’s this Intelligence right at the center with everything around it. But what’s so fascinating is that Apple held a major product launch event in September of the year 2026 and did not introduce a single notable new AI feature. The first 15 minutes or so of the keynote was simply a replay, a re-narrativization of what they introduced over the past two years with Apple Intelligence. And so they tried to just tell that story in a more concrete way. The other thing is they don’t have any AI devices at the very core, and so they need to prop up the iPhone as their AI device because they don’t have an alternative. But of course they’re only going to do that until they have that killer device, and then they’re going to change that whole narrative. So it’s a very narrative PR and marketing-driven company. And I’m not saying that to be critical. I mean, if I ran the company, obviously I’m going to tout what I have. I’m not going to veer from that. But it is interesting how they’re playing this. And I agree, they did play it very safe. There’s nothing safer than John Ternus introducing a new iPhone. It’s like the safest thing you can do. No major new AI product, no smart home hub, nothing in the spatial space, just straight down the middle. Yeah, it seems like that next wave of smart home products, which we’re expecting later this year… I say, “We’re expecting.” I’m expecting it because that is something you have reported. [Laughs] I am expecting it, yes. Mark Gurman is expecting new products from Apple. That is the first cut at some truly AI-native devices. Because you have Siri AI and it is functional now in a way that it previously was not functional, you can try some new classes of devices. There are about a half dozen AI-native devices coming in the next year and a half or so. The first will be the smart home hub, which is basically an Amazon Echo Show but Apple-style. It will have a square screen and an entirely new operating system. The idea is: what would a Siri AI operating system look like? This is that: intercom, video conferencing, proactive intelligence. So you walk up to it, it recognizes who you are, and it will show content personal to you. It will know who is speaking. Obviously, the Amazon Echo can do that, but Apple’s doing it in its own Apple-y way with AI-based Face ID. They’re working on a home security system. They’re working on another version of the smart home hub that I just talked about that is attached to a robotic arm. So you put it on your desk, and it can move around. It’s actually a category that’s pretty popping in Asia and in China right now. Then you’ve got the wearables, the smart glasses. I still believe those are going to be introduced and shipped in 2027, so not too far from now. Trust me, you’ll be wearing them. Within 365 days, you will be wearing them and have video footage of you wearing them at the Steve Jobs Theater. And if that is not the case, either something went horribly wrong for you or something went horribly wrong for Apple. You’ll also have the AirPods with cameras. That’s an interesting thing that we should talk about, but they’ll have the AirPods with cameras and then a few other wearables that I won’t get into. So this is what I was talking about when I said there were eras at Apple and people’s relationship with the company really changed. The Steve Jobs era was defined by devices, and in particular, Steve Jobs himself getting up and doing a keynote and famously putting up pictures of all the existing smartphones and saying, “Well, these all suck. And here’s the reason they all suck, and here’s the iPhone and here’s why it’s better.” That created one kind of relationship between Apple’s enormous community of fans, its leader, and the products. I think that was very successful. I think the Tim Cook era has been meaningfully different. I think it’s largely a story about scale. To some extent, it’s a story about values. To a huge extent, it’s a story about privacy. Apple has marketed itself as the privacy company. It fought the FBI to keep the iPhone encrypted. There’s a lot there with Tim Cook’s version of the company, but it’s more corporate. Certainly, it’s just a vaster company. It’s safer. It’s not as rough around the edges as Jobs’ Apple, but it wasn’t as device-based. I don’t think the Vision Pro has the same kind of mainstream cultural impact as even the hockey puck mouse that Jobs put out. There was a thing that he could do with products that Tim Cook Apple could not quite do with products. And that just feels really different to me. I’m going to correct you on that because every time I put an article or a post out about the Vision Pro being on life support, I get what amounts to basically a notch or two below a death threat from dozens of people. So people are passionate about it. Dozens? Dozens? Well, honestly, I think what it is is that people have created businesses around spatial computing and apps, and they’re just pissed off that they’ve invested all this time and money in a category that’s probably going to die out. And then you have consumers who spent four grand on this product, and they’re like, “I saved up for this thing, I’m living with this thing, and I’m pissed off to hear the realities.” But if you have another hour, we can talk about the Vision Pro. No, the comparison there is good. People have invested in it. They care deeply about it. The comparison I’m making is that the relationship people have to Apple in the Cook era is as an institution. It’s just like this big thing that spans the globe on a massive scale. It’s IBM. And then you’re going to do it with a pair of smart glasses, and you’re going to walk into all of the other things. Yeah. It feels like Apple knows that there’s a next generation of user interfaces coming that is AI-powered that requires an amount of ambient capture, whether that’s just listening so you can talk to it or whether it’s visual so you can see the world around you. And they haven’t solved the social privacy aspect. Nope. There are white papers about how Apple might have solved the technical database privacy aspect, right? Yep. They’ve got Private Cloud Compute, and they’re going to encrypt the data. They’re not going to store this and that. And I don’t think any of that’s going to overcome the social privacy aspect. They didn’t do a good job on articulating the social aspect of it at all. They could’ve shown more demos. They could’ve discussed it a bit deeper. I know they only have very limited time in the keynote, but I don’t think they spent enough time breaking things down here. I quite frankly think they did not do a good job rolling this feature out. I ask myself, would I be comfortable using this feature? Yeah. But then if I tell everyone around me in the last week, “Hey, I’ve been recording you the whole time,” they’re going to freak out, and they’re not going to trust Apple. So it’s a really interesting one. I’m pretty shocked they did it. What are the net new Apple Watch buyers because of this feature? What is the bigger challenge, doing this feature or not doing this feature? And I think that doing this feature is a bigger drawback than not doing the feature. Here, there is no cost of not doing something. Well, there is a cost if you think there’s about to be a wave of AI devices that are doing always-on transcripts and meeting recordings, and OpenAI is going to do something. I mean, we have seen a wave of startups that do this. But we’re not there yet, right? Right. This could’ve waited six months. So you can just foreclose it. This is like Microsoft stuff. You’re like, “Here’s a preview of a feature. Don’t even consider that stuff. Eventually this will get good,” and you’ve just foreclosed the competitor. Well, the other thing is they had nothing else for the watch, so they had to just do something, right? This is the weakest Apple Watch update we’ve seen in a long time, and they’re lost as to what to do next. Now they’re recalibrating it. They’re going to have a major watch revamp at the end of next year and so forth, but they have to do something. If it were me, I would have ripped off the bandaid at the same time with all the audio plus visual intelligence stuff next year. Do it all together and have a really coherent privacy story. But do you think that stuff is compatible with Apple’s reputation for privacy? This is the real question I’m getting at: they might not have told the right story about the Apple Watch. Apple is going to have to tell the right story about AirPods with cameras in them in a world where people are shooting spray foam at Flock cameras because they don’t want them in their communities. There’s a connection between these two ideas, and it doesn’t seem like Apple knows how to tell that story. Well, clearly not, because they haven’t done it. But here’s the story on the AirPods. They can’t record actual video. They can’t take actual pictures. They have an extremely low frame rate. I’m talking about a few frames per second. The actual data that gets input into them, it’s like… Have you ever used a Roomba, and when you look at the app, what does the Roomba see? It’s like wireframes of the environment. It would not be able to tell you and me apart. It’s just seeing two people. Then how can it do the brands of tomato sauce in the aisle? Well, in terms of non-people, it’d be able to do that, and it could read text. So it’d be pretty heavily reliant on reading text and seeing color and whatnot. But being able to differentiate between two people would be very difficult. It’s almost like a fake reproduction of what’s around you. I don’t have a good explanation for it, but I’m sure if they wanted to, they’ll give a good one. I’m not sure they’re going to break it down. They might just say, “Just trust us. We’re Apple. It’s not taking pictures. It’s not taking video. It doesn’t know what it’s seeing to some extent.” So we’ll see how they play it. But I would’ve done all this stuff together, ripped off the bandaid and spent a lot of time focused on it. There was no need to do this audio intelligence feature at the end of ’26 when you could have done it at the end of ’27. Unless you’re trying to slowly boil the frog, right? You’re going to get people mad about this, and then you’re going to do the next one the next time. Right. It just seems like this next generation of devices involves some kind of ambient listening that we are not ready for as a society. People are really mad about Meta glasses. What are you going to do about it? They soiled the water for Apple and a lot of other companies. Meta being the first mover on this created an industry-wide problem. And I think even though Apple has such a strong privacy stance, there are people who don’t believe them. There are people who don’t care what they have to say. There are people who are going to be angry about the Apple glasses and whatnot. I think Apple, to some extent, is on such a high horse with its privacy message that it came away surprised that there would be some backlash to Apple doing this. They think, I believe, that people are overblowing it when it comes to Apple and everyone should just be focused on Meta. And just because Meta has done a poor job protecting people’s privacy doesn’t mean we’re going to. So we’ll see what happens. One thing: when I talk to the folks there, they never make the connection between Apple and Meta in the sense that Meta’s apps run on Apple’s phones. People are mad about Meta, and they still think the phones, Apple’s phones, are listening to them, and they can’t quite make that connection because it undoes a lot of their own messaging. If you believe your iPhone is listening to you, that’s not just Meta’s problem. It is also Apple’s problem. They kind of have to actively ignore that relationship because otherwise everything else falls apart. And I think that’s why there’s this blind spot. If people’s watches start generating transcripts, it’s exactly the same relationship as “my iPhone is listening to me, and that’s why I saw an ad for a vacation that I only talked to my friend about.” I’m curious what they’re going to do. I have a feeling they’re just going to bulldoze their way through it. They’re going to just try to tell a good story. They’re going to do a ton of PR briefings about it. They’re going to do a ton of white papers about it, and get as nerdy and in-depth as they can on this stuff. You know what they’re going to do? They’re going to throw out a lot of comparisons. I even heard Ternus do this in one of the interviews, in Apple’s statement on some of these features. I could totally imagine them saying, “Why is it any different recording from smart glasses if you could just hold your phone up and record people?” With the audio intelligence feature, one thing I didn’t even think of is the Apple Watch- It’s very funny you just mentioned that because that is exactly what Mark Zuckerberg just said to our friend Alex Heath. Oh, that’s funny. “How is it different from a phone?” This is the industry’s approach. I think the answer is that people are like, “Yeah, I can see you doing that, and I feel very comfortable telling you to stop.” There’s something different about that. I didn’t even realize this. Someone pointed this out to me the other day. It’s like your Apple Watch has had the Voice Memos app for, I don’t know, eight years at this point. Who stopped anyone from recording their whole day with the Voice Memos app on the Apple Watch anyway? This is just a more privacy-centric version of that. So Apple’s solving a problem here. They’re not creating one. So it just depends on how you look at these things. I think they’ll bulldoze their way through it. It’s going to be a problem, but I think they’ll be fine. All right. Last two before I let you get out of here. We’ve talked around the iPhone Duo a lot. We’ve mentioned it a lot. It’s the thing that just came out. We haven’t talked about it. What do you think of it? I think it’s incredible. I think, and this is a bold take, that foldables will become the new normal within a decade. If you look at the market share of smartphones at the end of 2006, smartphones had like 6 percent of the market. Now they have 85 percent of the market. It went over 50 percent of the market after five to six years. The iPhone itself was not the source of that, but the iPhone got everyone into the smartphone game. I think the iPhone Duo is going to do the same for the phone market. I think it’s going to become the new normal. Even though Apple is a late mover to foldables? Yeah. I think the Apple brand is that strong, really. I really do. I think the fit and finish, the software integration, is going to get people really excited about this category. I think that the Apple Upgrade program, the leasing program, will eventually expand internationally. I think that’s going to get people in it. I think that at some point they’re going to stop advertising sticker prices and focus on the monthly prices, and they’re going to get people locked into this thing. They’re going to have a family of iPhone Duos over time. You’ll see every phone maker just transitioning, transitioning to foldables. Samsung: half the line is already foldables. Very soon the candy bar style is going to become legacy. That’s a big prediction. Although I will say their iPhone handoff feature, where you can move a number between phones, seems to point to a future where I, for example, have the folding phone for work and then a much smaller, lighter phone for the weekends with the family. You can see that vision taking shape only because it’s now easy to port a number between devices, just whenever you want, which I think is incredible. Last question. We’ve talked a lot about Apple, its culture, and its set of products. What do you think its biggest challenges are in the new era under John Ternus, and what do you think its biggest opportunities are? I would say that I think the biggest challenge and the biggest opportunity are the same thing. Ternus’ Apple for the next three to five years is still Tim Cook’s Apple, right? That’s just the reality. He’s still going to be there in the background. He’s still going to loom large, and the product pipeline is still going to be coming out of an era that started under Tim Cook. But in five years from now, they are going to need to start thinking of what actually replaces the iPhone as the next thing. We went from the Mac to iCloud to AI as the center. What is Apple’s new thing after the phone? What is Apple’s new thing after the current generation of AI? And Ternus’ tenure as CEO, I think, will go down as a success if he’s able to find that next new centerpiece. He’s got a few years before he needs to start cooking on that, but I’m talking about something that can be in development for 5 to 10 years. Tim Cook never had the opportunity to have his new centerpiece of the company. He never had the opportunity to put his stamp on products at the company for two reasons. Both things that he tried to do as his centerpiece failed spectacularly. Obviously the Vision Pro, but the car — the car, that was Apple’s multi-trillion-dollar market cap opportunity, and they just blew it. Ternus will need to successfully hit that. I’d actually put a third thing on that list. It was the very beginning of the Cook era, with Jobs literally on his deathbed, and he said he’d figured out TV. Oh, yes. He had to spend however long pretending he knew what that meant because I don’t think it had been solved. And so there was this first wave of “Apple’s going to redefine TV” because the last page of the Isaacson biography had a Jobs quote on it. They haven’t even done a new Apple TV box in four years. That’s a long time. It’s funny because you don’t need one. It never occurs to me that I need to upgrade this thing, but maybe there’s going to be some AI feature. Well, Siri AI. They’ve been waiting for the Siri AI update. This could be a whole other podcast, but Siri AI has been the gate to all of these new product categories. The AirPods were supposed to be out already, the Apple TV, the HomePod, the smart home hub… all these devices were supposed to come out. Apple couldn’t do any of them until Siri AI. Now Siri AI is here, so the floodgates are open. All right. Well, Mark, we’re going to have to have you back on the show to talk about those floodgates and all these new products very soon. I can’t believe you haven’t been on until now. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Yeah. And obviously I’d love to have you on my new podcast, Power On Podcast, launching very shortly. So thanks in advance. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

items.title: Reverse-Engineering Flock Cameras
items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content: Hackers captured a Flock camera and got a look (alternate link) at the software: While much of the automatic license plate reader’s (ALPR) most sensitive storage remained encrypted and inaccessible, the joint analysis of the recovered data shows that software running on the device explicitly detects people as well as vehicles, license plates, and bicycles. The camera can produce dozens of images of a single passing vehicle and, according to several weeks of recovered logs, generated more than a million images. Its computer-vision software also sometimes isolated bumper stickers and other graphics, including, in one case, an American flag patch on a motorcyclist’s saddlebag. If you’re wondering how the hackers got by disk encryption, one of the unencrypted partitions contained the key for an encrypted partition. That’s pretty bad security engineering.

items.title: 🎙️ How I AI: Meta’s Muse review + How Warp ships 2,000 PRs a month with AI factories
items.author: Lenny Rachitsky
items.content: Muse review: The personal AI agent that gets consumer UX rightListen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple PodcastsBrought to you by:Optimizely—Your AI agent orchestration platform for marketing and digital teamsOpenArt—An all-in-one AI creation platform for images, videos, music, audio, and moreIn this solo episode, Claire tests Meta’s Muse, a personal AI agent designed for everyday users. She walks through how it manages her family calendar, creates a polished morning newsletter, tracks personal goals, and asks for permission before acting on sensitive information. She also explores the thoughtful details that make Muse feel trustworthy, where its browser use still falls short, and what its approach could mean for the future of consumer AI.Biggest takeaways:Meta’s consumer design expertise makes Muse feel different from other agents on the market. The teams behind Facebook and Instagram understand how to build trust with nontechnical users, and that experience shows up throughout Muse. It never exposed Claire to a terminal, surfaced a confusing error, or requested permission at an awkward moment. She tested onboarding, calendar management, email ingestion, goal setting, and browser-based purchasing in one session without encountering a single moment of friction that broke the experience.Muse created the best version of Claire’s family morning brief on its first attempt. Claire has tested generating family newsletters with OpenClaw and Codex, but Muse produced a more beautiful and thoughtfully structured PDF without requiring any follow-up prompting. It even added a “Talk at the Table” section with kid-friendly questions about the news and proactively identified scheduling conflicts. That is the standard personal agents should aim for: not simply completing the request but noticing useful things the user did not think to ask about.How an agent requests permission matters as much as what it can do once permission is granted. Muse does not default to unlimited access or interrupt the user with constant approval requests. It asks at the moment access becomes relevant, confirms what it found, and checks again before taking action. After reading Claire’s email to build a family profile, for example, Muse summarized what it had learned and asked whether it could use that information. Anyone building an agent that handles personal data should pay attention to that interaction pattern.Muse’s activity feed provides the kind of agent transparency Claire wants everywhere. Every task includes a detailed record of the tool calls, scripts, searches, and individual steps Muse completed. Most consumers will probably ignore it, but developers and power users will find it invaluable. Claire immediately wanted the same interface in Codex and Claude Code. Seeing exactly how an agent arrived at an outcome builds a different level of trust than receiving a polished result with no visibility into the process.Personal goals require a different product model than tasks or chat. Helping someone gently sleep-train an eight-and-a-half-month-old while room-sharing in a small house is not a request that can be completed in one sitting. Muse gathered context across multiple turns, established a reminder, and treated the situation as an ongoing goal whose progress should be tracked. Its tone was warm and specific without becoming overly agreeable. Claire said she felt “zero percent annoyed” with it, which she described as a miracle.Browser use remains the weak link for consumer agents. Muse struggled to shop for New Balance 9060s in a specific colorway, returning incorrect results and failing to complete the purchase. It performed better while buying tickets for The Odyssey, but initially opened the wrong movie. These failures are not unique to Muse. They are a reminder that browser-based shopping remains unreliable across the entire agent category.Muse’s animated avatar shows what it means to design specifically for AI. Instead of displaying a generic spinner while it works, Muse generates an animation in which its avatar picks up a tiny laptop when completing tasks and an orb when creating media. Nobody asked for this feature, but it makes the agent’s state immediately understandable. For Claire, this is what operating at the top of the craft looks like. It is not just polished corners and clean icons. It is using capabilities like image generation and animation to solve experience problems that could not have been solved before.Muse is introducing a new vocabulary for consumer AI. It avoids technical terms such as crons, tools, artifacts, plugins, and connectors. Instead, it organizes the product around a feed, ideas, goals, and a library. That language is a deliberate design decision. The words a product uses determine who feels comfortable using it, and Muse is clearly designed for a much broader audience than today’s coding and productivity agents are.Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode:Meta Muse Review: A Personal AI Agent for Family Life: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/meta-muse-review-personal-ai-agent↳ How to Create a Printable Family Newsletter with Meta Muse: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/meta-muse-printable-family-newsletter↳ How to Set Personal Goals and Reminders with Meta Muse: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/meta-muse-personal-goals-reminders↳ How to Find and Buy Movie Tickets with Meta Muse: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/meta-muse-movie-ticketsHow Warp ships 2,000 PRs a month with AI factories | Zach Lloyd (CEO, Warp)Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple PodcastsBrought to you by:DX—Engineering intelligence for the AI eraOpenArt—An all-in-one AI creation platform for images, videos, music, audio, and moreZach Lloyd is the co-founder and CEO of Warp, an agentic development platform for software teams. In this episode, he demonstrates how Warp Factories turns a request in Slack into a tracked, tested, and merged pull request, with the first PR ready in as little as 35 minutes. He also explains how the team measures human involvement, scores every agent run, replays real tasks to compare models, and uses failed runs to continuously improve the factory itself.Biggest takeaways:A software factory is not just a faster coding agent. It is the entire development lifecycle running in the cloud. Warp’s factory, Wilson, can take a request from Slack through triage, Linear ticket creation, implementation, pull-request creation, computer-use QA, and merge without a human touching the keyboard. The difference between a factory and a coding agent is the difference between an assembly line and a single machinist. One completes a task. The other coordinates the entire production process.“Human interactions per pull request” may be the clearest measure of factory efficiency. Every follow-up prompt in Slack, clarification on a Linear ticket, and correction during code review represents additional human effort. Zach believes that the more steering an agent requires, the lower the factory’s true throughput becomes. It does not matter how quickly the agent writes code if a human remains the rate limiter, yet most teams are not measuring this.Humans in code review are now the biggest bottleneck in Warp’s engineering process. Wilson takes an average of 35 minutes to move from kickoff to pull request. The first human review arrives 3.5 hours later. Warp has already removed one source of delay by allowing the person who prompted the agent to review its work instead of requiring a separate reviewer. The company has not eliminated human review entirely, but Zach expects that accumulated trust will eventually make it possible for selected changes to merge without human review.A company’s own past work provides a better model benchmark than a public leaderboard. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench measure performance on generic tasks. Warp instead replays real factory jobs using different model configurations, evaluates them with the same judging system used in production, and maps the cost-quality tradeoff on a Pareto chart. For Warp’s workload, model selection is the largest cost lever by far, with context management a distant second.Software factories can improve themselves when their configuration lives in code. Warp’s improvement loop collects failed runs until there is enough evidence to identify a pattern, typically around 20 to 25 examples. An observer agent analyzes what went wrong and proposes changes to the factory’s agent definitions. Because those definitions are stored as code, the same agents that complete the work can also update the instructions governing how they operate.The scoring layer is what separates a reliable factory from a vibe-coded pipeline. Warp uses an AI judge to score every agent run across multiple dimensions, including whether it created redundant tests. Agents often write tests that merely confirm current behavior instead of protecting against future regressions. The judging model is intentionally mid-tier so evaluation costs do not erase the factory’s savings, and Warp can adjust the sampling rate depending on how much oversight a workflow needs.AI becomes far more valuable outside engineering when it connects to real business data. During the conversation, Zach ran three tasks in parallel: redesigning a slide through Figma, extracting the 10 most common sales questions from four weeks of Granola transcripts, and creating a cold-lead re-engagement list in Google Sheets. The redesigned slide was useful, but the Granola analysis was more consequential. It identified “buy versus build” as the top customer question and backed that conclusion with evidence, giving Warp a clear signal about what its website and sales deck should address next.Working with agents in public can spread expertise without a formal training program. Every Wilson task runs in a shared Slack channel, allowing junior employees to watch experienced users prompt, steer, and correct the system in real time. Zach sees a power-law effect in agent usage: a small number of people become dramatically better than everyone else. Making their workflows visible allows those skills to spread quietly across the organization.Building faster does not help if the team builds the wrong thing. Warp still relies on user interviews, design sessions, and direct observation of how people use the product. The factory dramatically accelerates implementation, but it does not decide what deserves to be built or why. Those decisions still depend on human taste, customer understanding, and product judgment. The build phase may be changing quickly, but the work that comes before it remains remarkably traditional.Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode:Inside Warp’s Software Factory: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/inside-warps-software-factory↳ How to Build an Automated Software Factory: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/how-to-build-an-automated-software-factory↳ How to Build an AI-Powered CEO Toolkit: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/how-to-build-an-ai-powered-ceo-toolkit↳ How to Measure and Self-Improve Your AI Software Development Factory: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/how-to-measure-and-self-improve-your-ai-software-development-factoryIf you’re enjoying these episodes, reply and let me know what you’d love to learn more about: AI workflows, hiring, growth, product strategy—anything.Catch you next week,LennyP.S. Want every new episode delivered the moment it drops? Hit “Follow” on your favorite podcast app.

items.title: Grab an Xbox controller and a $50 Xbox gift card together for just $80

items.content: Newegg is hosting a bundle that includes Microsoft’s wireless Xbox controller (in black) and a $50 digital Xbox gift card together for $80. Given that this model typically sits around $50 to $60 depending on the color you want, this is a fantastic value since it essentially knocks its price down to $30. items.title: Open-Sourcing Rebalancer: A Generic, High-Performance Library for Solving Assignment Problems
items.content: We’re open-sourcing Rebalancer, the assignment-problem solver that has been used to solve resource allocation problems throughout Meta for over nine years. Rebalancer separates several related concerns: how to specify an assignment problem, how to store it efficiently in memory, how to solve it, and how to debug it. This separation of concerns is crucial to Rebalancer’s usability, scalability, and extensibility. For a more detailed technical exposition, see the accompanying paper, “Optimizing Resource Allocation in Hyperscale Datacenters: Scalability, Usability, and Experiences,” published at OSDI’24. Given a set of objects and a set of bins, how do we assign objects to bins in a way that optimizes specific objectives while meeting certain constraints? This question arises at all layers of Meta’s infrastructure stack including in Hardware placement: racks (objects) need to be positioned in datacenters (bins) to optimize the spread of racks across electrical fault domains while honoring power and cooling limitations. Service placement: servers (objects) need to be assigned to services (bins) in order to meet each service’s demand while optimizing for goals such as fault tolerance (spread a service’s allocated servers across failure domains) and packing efficiency. Task placement: tasks (objects) need to be allocated to servers (bins) while honoring server resource limits and optimizing for goals such as fault tolerance and co-location requirements. Traffic routing: Route traffic (objects) from billions of users to geographically distributed datacenters (bins) while optimizing network latency and datacenter load. The main challenges to designing a reusable framework for solving problems like these are its usability and scalability. Usability is impeded by practitioners struggling to translate real-life policies into the precise mathematical formulas required by formal optimization methods, while scalability is hampered by NP-hard problems that cannot be solved efficiently by commercial solvers. Rebalancer addresses both of these challenges by separating a problem’s specification from its solution. Rebalancer provides a language for describing problems using objects, bins, constraints, and objectives, as in the examples above. Once a problem is described in this way, Rebalancer transforms the problem into a directed-acyclic graph called an expression graph. Rebalancer’s solving algorithm uses the expression graph to either design a local search heuristic or to build a mixed integer program (MIP) solvable with either a commercial (FICO Xpress or Gurobi) or open source solver (HiGHS). Specifying Assignment Problems Rebalancer’s specification language employs a three-step approach to incrementally elevate the level of abstraction for ease of use. First, it introduces essential modeling constructs, such as dimensions (the real-world attributes of objects and bins), partitions (groupings of objects), scopes (groupings of bins), and utilization (contribution of objects assigned to a bin). Next, Rebalancer provides an API to expose commonly used expressions for transformations on these constructs, as well as recursively on other expressions. For example, the utilization of several bins can be aggregated using a SUM/MAX operation, or transformed using a SQUARE operation. Finally, leveraging these expressions, Rebalancer exposes a high-level spec API implementing dozens of common objectives and constraints. One can think of each spec as a predefined recipe which accepts some modeling constructs and additional parameters as input, and creates a mathematical formula using the expression API. An example of modeling constructs and specs for a task placement problem. In the example above, tasks are modeled as objects and servers are modeled as bins into which tasks are to be placed. Servers are physically situated in racks; this grouping is modeled as a scope. Tasks take a certain amount of CPU and storage and servers have a limited amount of each. CPU and storage are modeled as dimensions. The CPU and storage utilization of a server corresponds to the sum of all of the tasks assigned to that server and the server’s utilization limits are modeled using a CapacitySpec. The expression API could be used to change how the utilization is calculated if a simple sum isn’t appropriate. Further, we model tasks as belonging to jobs. A grouping of objects like this is called a partition and we use a GroupCountSpec to ensure that each rack has only a single job type (partition) assigned to it. A BalanceSpec ensures that each server’s utilization is balanced across both its CPU and storage dimensions. This example demonstrates how complex assignment problems can be easily and naturally constructed using Rebalancer and how specs provide a way of expressing constraints and goals that can be re-used in many different ways by varying dimensions, scopes, or partitions. Please check out an exhaustive list of Rebalancer specs in the docs. Solving Assignment Problems Once a problem is specified using the API described above, Rebalancer translates it into an expression graph. The leaf nodes in this graph represent utilization expressions; for example, the memory utilization of server A, as obtained by summing the memory contribution of tasks assigned to server A. These utilization values are then recursively composed using aggregation nodes such as Max and Sum, or transformation nodes such as Square and Abs. Note that the value of each node in the expression graph depends on the current assignment and needs to be updated every time the assignment changes. Along with the problem objectives and constraints, modelers also provide Rebalancer with an initial assignment and a stopping condition, such as a time limit. Rebalancer will compute an optimized assignment that minimizes the objective value and does not violate any new constraints. The constraints that were violated by the initial assignment become high priority goals and their violation is minimized, ideally to zero. Rebalancer offers two distinct techniques to solve the assignment problem. Optimal Solver. In this mode, Rebalancer translates the expression graph into a set of expressions that can be fed into MIP solvers such as FICO Xpress, Gurobi, or HiGHS. During this translation, Rebalancer needs to represent utilization of a bin by a weighted sum of binary decision variables (one per object) that indicate if the object is assigned to the bin; this can lead to very large MIP models! Rebalancer automatically uses techniques such as variable aggregation (compacting similar objects into a single integer variable), interchangeability, and symmetry breaking to reduce model sizes, but the worst case size of the generated MIP model can still be quadratic, i.e. O(|objects| * |bins|). The largest problems we consider are too big for any MIP solver. Local Search Solver overcomes this limitation by working directly on the expression graph, exploring the local neighborhood around the current assignment by moving some objects to another bin. This neighborhood has a worst-case size of O(|objects|+|bins|), which allows Rebalancer to model even very large problems without hitting memory limitations. Each move creates a new candidate assignment for which Rebalancer evaluates the new values of the objectives and constraints. After all candidates have been evaluated, Rebalancer applies the best candidate assignment; that is, the one that does not violate a constraint and improves the objective by the maximum amount. This process of evaluating and applying moves is repeated until no progress can be made or a stopping condition is reached. Rebalancer’s local search algorithm is heavily optimized and parallelized so that each evaluation is relatively inexpensive (millions of evaluations per second are possible), allowing us to quickly explore the search space. In addition, Rebalancer knows how to prune the search space, cutting down the number of evaluations needed in the first place. The right solution technique will depend on your needs. At Meta, almost all large-scale problems use local search. Small- to mid-size problems that have moderate solve time requirements often use the optimal solver. It is also common to prototype with the optimal solver and then migrate to local search after a high-quality baseline solution has been identified. Offline, the optimal solver can be used to tune local search. Rebalancer at Meta For the last decade, Rebalancer has been continuously used and improved at Meta. It is used to solve a wide range of infrastructure optimization problems including assigning shards to servers (Shard Manager), servers to services (RAS), routing traffic from globally distributed edge datacenters to main datacenters (Taiji), grouping serverless functions to improve locality, balancing online ML training workloads across regions while considering the priority of ML workloads, and so on. At the time of this writing, Rebalancer is used to solve roughly 40 million assignment problems every day with more than 30 unique problem formulations. The P99 solve time is 12 seconds on a problem with 265k objects and 3.2k bins. For problems with more than 1 million objects and 5k bins, the average solve time is 171 seconds and there are more than 3.4k such runs. Unsurprisingly, Rebalancer has also been used to solve non-infrastructure problems such as assigning meetings to meeting rooms to minimize travel time, assigning support tickets to engineers, and optimizing desk placements. Beyond Meta, assignment problems arise in many domains such as healthcare, energy and utilities, transportation and logistics, education, and emergency response, and, while we don’t have the expertise to apply Rebalancer to these areas ourselves, we hope that others do and will. Debugging With Rebalancer making it easy to formulate and solve problems, we found that the majority of engineering time for modelers shifted to debugging the solver’s behavior. Without proper tools, such debugging required a deep understanding of the solver’s internals. Over time we identified common questions and pain points among modelers and built a specialized UI tool for answering them: Rebalancer Explorer. https://facebook.github.io/rebalancer/videos/rebalancer-explorer-demo.mp4 Explorer accompanies Rebalancer in this open-source release as a Dockerized web UI that facilitates rapid debugging and iteration when solving problems with both local search and optimal solvers. It helps answer questions such as which constraints are binding, what would happen if a constraint were relaxed, and why an object was placed in one bin and not another. The Future of Rebalancer We are always looking to optimize Rebalancer’s performance, add new capabilities, and extend it to support a wider range of assignment problems. Rebalancer is proud to be open-source (Apache 2.0 license) and we invite both systems and optimization experts to try Rebalancer and contribute to the project by identifying performance bottlenecks, adding new solve techniques, extending it to support new sorts of problems, or just by fixing bugs. We look forward to seeing how the systems and optimization communities adopt, build, and contribute to Rebalancer. Code: Rebalancer GitHub repo Docs: Introducing to Rebalancer PyPI: Rebalancer Python package Paper: Optimizing Resource Allocation in Hyperscale Datacenters: Scalability, Usability, and Experiences — OSDI 2024 Acknowledgements Rebalancer was developed by past and present members of the Algorithmic Optimization team at Meta: Pol Mauri Ruiz, Igor Kabiljo, Neeraj Kumar, Vijay Menon, Mayank Pundir, Andrew Newell, Liyuan Wang, Richard Barnes, Sahil Deshpande, Karthik Velakur, Yang Liu, Leart Gjoni, Ravi Surulikamu, Tony Zhang, Raj Rajendran, Aravind Narayanan, Lakshmi Ganesh, and Saranyan Vigraham. The post Open-Sourcing Rebalancer: A Generic, High-Performance Library for Solving Assignment Problems appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
